source.rationale: Preserves the disputed ordering of the earliest converts and the qualified claim that Khadijah was the first woman to embrace Islam.

items.english_text:
Who was the first to embrace Islam? There are several opinions: it is said that it was Abu Bakr; it is said, Ali; it is said, Zayd; and it is said, Khadijah. The sound view is that Abu Bakr was the first free man to embrace Islam. This was stated by Ibn Abbas, Hassan, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, and others. Supporting this is Muslim's narration from Amr ibn Abasa in the account of his conversion and his question to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): “Who is with you in this?” He replied: “A free man and a slave.” He said: With him that day were Abu Bakr and Bilal, among those who believed in him. [(1)]

Al-Hakim narrated in al-Mustadrak, by way of Khalid ibn Sa'id, who said: Al-Sha'bi was asked, “Who was the first to embrace Islam?” He replied: “Have you not heard Hassan's words?” [al-Basit]

If you recall grief arising from a trusted brother,
remember your brother Abu Bakr for what he did.

For he is the best of creation, its most God-fearing and just,
after the Prophet, and the most faithful to what he undertook;

The second, the one who followed, whose presence is praised,
and the first among the people to believe the Messenger.

Al-Tabarani narrated in al-Kabir from al-Sha'bi, who said: I asked Ibn Abbas, and he related it. [(2)]

Ibn al-Salah said: “The more scrupulous formulation is to say: the first free man to embrace Islam was Abu Bakr; the first boy, Ali; the first woman, Khadijah; the first client, Zayd; and the first slave, Bilal.”

Al-Birmawi said: “This reconciliation is also related from Abu Hanifa.” Ibn Khalawayh said: “The first woman to embrace Islam after Khadijah was Lubaba bint al-Harith, the wife of al-Abbas.”

_________
[(1)] Muslim included it in al-Sahih, 1/569, Book of the Prayer of Travelers and Its Abbreviation (6), chapter on the conversion of Amr ibn Abasa (52), hadith no. 294/832; al-Nasa'i in al-Sunan, 1/283, Book of Prayer (5), chapter on the permissibility of prayer until the dawn prayer is performed (40), hadith no. 584; Ibn Majah in al-Sunan, 1/434, Book of Establishing the Prayer and the Sunna Concerning It (5), chapter concerning which hours of the night are best (182), hadith no. 1364; Ahmad in al-Musnad, 4/111, 112, 113, 114, 385; al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan, 2/454 and 6/369; Ibn Sa'd, 4/1/157–158; and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, 2/16. Al-Bayhaqi mentioned it in al-Zawa'id, 1/57, 63, and Ibn Abd al-Barr in al-Tamhid, 4/14, 24.
[(2)] Tadrib al-Rawi, 2/225–226.

decisions.issue: Meaning of شجوا in Hassan's first verse
decisions.resolution: Rendered as “grief,” without retaining an unresolved item.
decisions.basis: The word's ordinary poetic sense is adequate in context; its range between grief, sorrow, and longing does not make the Arabic text damaged.

source.rationale: Substantively records uncertainty over the identity of a reported nephew and conflicting information about Khadijah’s brothers.

items.english_text:
97—Asad ibn Khuwaylid [(3)]

In Khadijah's lineage [(4)]

Muhammad ibn Jabir narrated his hadith from Simak and from someone who heard Asad ibn Khuwaylid. This is how Ibn Manda mentioned him. Abu Umar said: “Asad, Khadijah's nephew, narrated from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) that he said: ‘Do not sell what you do not possess.’”

Al-Uqayli mentioned him and said: “There is criticism concerning its chain of transmission.”

End quote. The genealogists mention no brother of Khadijah apart from al-Awwam, al-Zubayr's father, who died during the pre-Islamic period, and Nawfal, who was killed at Badr as an unbeliever. It is said that his nephew al-Zubayr killed him, and it is said that Ali killed him. It is therefore possible that this Asad was a son of Nawfal, although they did not mention that.

_________
[(3)] Tajrid Asma' al-Sahaba, 1/14; Usd al-Ghaba, entry 90; al-Isti'ab, entry 26.
[(4)] Manuscript J reads: “a relative of Khadijah.”

decisions.issue: Variant heading نسيب خديجة
decisions.resolution: Retained the printed heading and translated the manuscript-J variant in footnote [(4)].
decisions.basis: Both readings are intelligible and the supplied Arabic expressly records their textual relationship.

source.rationale: Adds migration history for Khadijah’s nephew and notes that his father Nوفل persecuted Muslims in the early period.

items.english_text:
171—Al-Aswad ibn Nawfal [(2)]

Ibn Khuwaylid ibn Asad ibn Abd al-Uzza ibn Qusayy, the Qurashi al-Asadi and Khadijah's nephew. He was among those who emigrated to Abyssinia in the second emigration; Ibn Ishaq mentioned him. His mother was Furay'a bint Adi ibn Nawfal ibn Abd Manaf. He emigrated to Medina after the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) arrived. He was the grandfather of Abu al-Aswad Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad, the ward of Urwa. His father, Nawfal, was harsh toward the Muslims at the beginning of Islam.

_________
[(2)] Al-Iqd al-Thamin, 3/317; Usd al-Ghaba, entry 155; al-Isti'ab, entry 41.

items.english_text:
399—[Ibrahim, son of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) [(3)]

Another [person]. Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn al-Junayd al-Razi mentioned in his History—which is a small volume—that Khadijah bore the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) his four daughters. Then, after the daughters, she bore al-Qasim, al-Tahir, Ibrahim, and al-Tayyib. The boys died while they were still nursing. He did not mention Mariya the Copt. In his account he said: “She bore Ibrahim, and he died young.” I have not seen this stated by anyone else, and he did not mention

_________
[(3)] Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, 1/134; Tahdhib al-Asma' wa-l-Lughat, 1/102; Tajrid Asma' al-Sahaba, 1/8; Ma'rifat al-Sahaba, 2/142.

decisions.issue: Sentence and editorial bracket continue in the next supplied passage
decisions.resolution: Preserved the open bracket and incomplete sentence exactly as a passage boundary.
decisions.basis: The following supplied result provides the continuation, so the underlying Arabic is not unresolved.

source.rationale: Continues Ibn Hajar’s qualification of the exceptional report, explaining it as a probable confusion between Khadijah and Mariya.

items.english_text:
Mariya and the son he had by her. What he mentioned was not an unmitigated error; rather, his mind may have shifted, so that he supposed all the children were by Khadijah and overlooked Mariya.] [(1)]

_________
[(1)] Omitted in manuscripts A, J, and D.

decisions.issue: Opening phrase مارية وما له منها
decisions.resolution: Corrected “Mariya, or the child he had by her” to “Mariya and the son he had by her.”
decisions.basis: The Arabic conjunction is و, and the phrase completes the preceding passage's “he did not mention.”

decisions.resolution: Rendered as “his mind may have shifted.”
decisions.basis: This preserves the explanatory possibility without presenting the conjecture as certain.

source.rationale: Adds a report about Muhammad’s journey in Khadijah’s trade with Maysara and Bahira’s alleged recognition of prophetic signs.

items.english_text: In Abu Sa'id al-Naysaburi's Sharaf al-Mustafa it is also related that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) passed by Bahira when he went out to trade on Khadijah's behalf, accompanied by Maysara. Bahira said to him: “I have recognized all the signs in you except the seal of prophethood, so uncover your back for me.” He uncovered his back, and Bahira saw it. He then said: “I testify that there is no god but God, and I testify that you are God's Messenger, the unlettered Prophet of whom Jesus son of Mary gave glad tidings.” He then related the account at very great length. God knows best.

decisions.issue: Nature of the trading journey
decisions.resolution: Rendered في تجارة خديجة as “to trade on Khadijah's behalf.”
decisions.basis: This conveys the agency expressed by the Arabic more precisely than merely “a trading journey for Khadijah.”

source.rationale: Preserves a chronologically significant report connecting Abu Bakr, Khadijah’s marriage, and Ali’s birth, despite its unusual formulation.

items.english_text:
Maymun ibn Mihran said: “Abu Bakr had indeed believed in the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) since the time [(1)] of Bahira the monk. Abu Bakr acted as an intermediary between him and Khadijah until he married her. That was before Ali was born.”

_________
[(1)] Manuscript A reads: “at the time.”

decisions.issue: Elliptical clause واختلف بينه وبين خديجة
decisions.resolution: Rendered Abu Bakr as acting as an intermediary between the Prophet and Khadijah.
decisions.basis: The context supplies Abu Bakr as the agent and Muhammad as the antecedent of the pronoun; the idiom denotes repeated mediation between two parties.

decisions.issue: Variant من زمن / في زمن
decisions.resolution: Retained “since the time” in the text and “at the time” in the footnote.
decisions.basis: This follows the printed text while preserving manuscript A's reading.

source.rationale: Adds a distinct revelation narrative in which Khadijah cites pre-marriage predictions and consults a monk, Addas, and Waraqa.

items.english_text:
Sulayman al-Taymi also mentioned it. He said: “It has reached us that the first thing with which God specially distinguished Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) was that he saw a vision at Hira [(1)], to which he used to withdraw in flight from what they did with their gods. Gabriel descended to him and drew near, and Muhammad became afraid of him.” He then related the hadith. Khadijah said to him: “Rejoice, for you are the prophet of this community. Before I married you, Nasih, my servant, and Bahira the monk informed me of this.” She then left him and went to the monk, who told her: “Gabriel is God's messenger and His trusted emissary to the messengers.” She then departed from him and came to a Christian slave of Utba ibn Rabi'a, a man from Nineveh called Addas. She told him [what had happened], and he told her the same. Then she went to Waraqa.

Musa ibn Uqba also related this account. In his version Addas said: “He is God's trusted intermediary between Him and the prophets, and the companion of Moses and Jesus.”

Ibn A'idh also related in al-Maghazi, by way of Uthman ibn Ata, from his father, from Ikrima, from Ibn Abbas, a similar account in full.

_________
[(1)] Hira, with a kasra and without gemination, is one of the mountains of Mecca. See Mu'jam al-Buldan, 2/269.

decisions.issue: Temporal object of قبل أن أتزوج
decisions.resolution: Rendered it as “Before I married you.”
decisions.basis: Khadijah is addressing Muhammad, and the report concerns predictions made before their marriage.

decisions.issue: Ellipsis in فقالت له
decisions.resolution: Supplied “[what had happened]” in editorial brackets.
decisions.basis: The Arabic clearly denotes her telling Addas the preceding matter, while leaving its object unstated.

source.rationale: Identifies a maternal cousin through Khadijah’s mother and supplies substantive, conflicting migration and later-life information about him.

items.english_text:
Humayr ibn Mu'ays ibn Amir ibn Lu'ayy, the Qurashi of the Banu Amir.

His mother, Umm Maktum, was Atika bint Abd Allah ibn Ankatha—the latter name beginning with an undotted ayn, followed by a vowelless nun, and with a three-dotted tha after the kaf—ibn A'idh ibn Makhzum. He was Khadijah, Mother of the Believers', maternal cousin, for Khadijah's mother, whose name was Fatima, was the sister of Qays ibn Za'ida. He embraced Islam early in Mecca and was among the earliest emigrants. He arrived in Medina before the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) emigrated. It is also said that he arrived after him, shortly after the Battle of Badr; this was stated by al-Waqidi.

The first view is sounder. It has been narrated by way of Abu Ishaq from al-Bara, who said: “The first emigrant to come to us was Mus'ab ibn Umayr; then Ibn Umm Maktum arrived.” The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) used to appoint him as his deputy over Medina during most of his military expeditions, and he would lead the people in prayer.

Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar said: “He went out to al-Qadisiyya, participated in the fighting, and was martyred there. He was carrying the standard at the time.” It is also said that he returned to Medina after al-Qadisiyya and died there; al-Baghawi mentioned this.

Al-Waqidi said instead: “He participated in it, returned to Medina, and died there. No mention of him was heard after Umar ibn al-Khattab.”

He narrated from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), and his hadith appears in the Sunan collections.

Abd Allah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Had, Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, Abu Razin al-Asadi, and others narrated from him.

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: “A group of scholars of genealogy and the military campaigns related that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) appointed Ibn Umm Maktum as his deputy thirteen times: at al-Abwa, Buwat, Dhu al-Ashira, his expedition in pursuit of Kurz ibn Jabir, the expedition of al-Sawiq, Ghatafan, the expedition of Uhud, Hamra al-Asad, Najran, Dhat al-Riqa, when he departed for the Farewell Pilgrimage, and when he departed for Badr. He then appointed Abu Lubaba instead when he sent Ibn Umm Maktum back from the road.” He said: “As for Qatada's narration from Anas that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) appointed Ibn Umm Maktum as his deputy, the number that reached him did not reach the number reported by others.” End quote.

He is the person mentioned in the sura, “He frowned and turned away” [Abasa 80:1], and concerning him was revealed, “except those with disability” [al-Nisa 4:95], when “Those believers who remain seated are not equal…” [al-Nisa 4:95] was revealed. Al-Bukhari included it.

In the Sunan, by way of Asim ibn Abi Razin, Ibn Umm Maktum said: “I said, ‘O Messenger of God, I am a blind man…’” followed by the hadith emphasizing communal prayer. God knows best.

source.rationale: Places Muhammad in Khadijah’s house when Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf came to him at the beginning of the mission.

items.english_text:
Al-Balawi narrated his hadith from Umara ibn Zayd, from Abd Allah ibn al-Ala, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman, who said: Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman used to say: I heard my father say:

“I traveled to Yemen one year before the prophetic mission and stayed with Asqalan ibn Awakin al-Himyari. He was a very old man whose life had been prolonged until he had become like a fledgling, and he would say:

When an old man grows deaf and can no longer speak, [(1)]
and his hearing is gone, leaving only his hands [for communication];

that is an illness for which there is no cure
apart from death, which gives voice to calamities.

I witnessed among us, alongside kings, men of our own [uncertain],
and lived to see the decisive stations in affairs.

They all perished, and I became a housebound fixture,
cast down, speaking to no one in the secluded chambers [uncertain]. [al-Wafir]

Abd al-Rahman said: Whenever I arrived, I would stay with him, and he would continually ask me about Mecca and its circumstances and whether anyone had appeared there who opposed their religion. Eventually I returned from the journey during which the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) had been commissioned while I was away. I stayed with him. He sat with a bandage tied over his eyes and said to me: ‘State your lineage, brother of Quraysh.’ I replied: ‘I am Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf ibn Abd Awf ibn Abd al-Harith ibn Zuhra.’ He said: ‘That is enough.’ Then he said: ‘Shall I give you glad tidings that are better for you than trade?’ I replied: ‘Yes.’ He said: ‘I bring you a wondrous report and give you glad tidings of something greatly to be desired. In the first month, God raised up a prophet from your people whom He approved as His chosen one. He sent down to him a complete Book. He forbids idols and summons to Islam; he commands the truth and practices it, and forbids falsehood and abolishes it. He is from the Banu Hashim, and your clan are indeed his maternal kinsmen. Abd al-Rahman, support him and affirm him, and convey these verses to him:

I bear witness by God, Possessor of the heights
and Cleaver of the night and morning,

that you are of the innermost stock of Quraysh,
and the son of the man redeemed from slaughter.

You have been sent to summon people to certainty,
guiding them to truth and success.

The repeated passage of the years has broken my strength,
preventing repeated travel by evening and morning.

I bear witness by God, the Lord of Moses,
that you were sent in the valleys of Mecca.

So be my intercessor before a Sovereign
who summons created beings to righteousness. [Mukhalla al-Basit]

Abd al-Rahman said: I returned and met Abu Bakr, who was my close associate. I told him the news, and he said: ‘This is Muhammad ibn Abd Allah. God has sent him as a messenger to His creation, so go to him.’ I went to him, and he was in Khadijah's house.

_________
[(1)] Manuscript H reads: “does not talk.”

unresolved.location: Asqalan's first poem, especially إلا يدايا, شهدت بنا مع الأملاك منا, and لا أبوح إلى الخلايا
unresolved.issue: The transmitted wording remains syntactically and lexically uncertain. The alternative editions confirm most of the same difficult readings, although they improve جلسا to حلسا. They therefore do not securely establish the meaning of the other phrases.
unresolved.best_rendering: “and his hearing is gone, leaving only his hands [for communication] … I witnessed among us, alongside kings, men of our own [uncertain] … I became a housebound fixture, cast down, speaking to no one in the secluded chambers [uncertain].”
unresolved.human_question: Can a manuscript facsimile or an earlier source for Asqalan's poem establish alternative readings for إلا يدايا, شهدت بنا, or الخلايا?

decisions.issue: Sequence expressed by قدمت القدمة التي بعث النبي وأنا غائب فيها
decisions.resolution: Corrected it to “I returned from the journey during which the Prophet had been commissioned while I was away.”
decisions.basis: The narrator departed before the mission and returned after the commissioning; قدمت describes his return, not his arrival upon a journey.

decisions.issue: Reading جلسا in the fourth verse
decisions.resolution: Adopted the collateral editions' reading حلسا and rendered it “a housebound fixture.”
decisions.basis: Both alternative editions independently transmit حلسا, which is metrically and idiomatically intelligible, whereas جلسا is defective here.

decisions.issue: Other difficult wording in the first poem
decisions.resolution: Retained explicit uncertainty in the translation and in a human-facing unresolved item.
decisions.basis: The available witnesses repeat the same difficult readings and do not justify the blind translation's confident resolution.

source.rationale: Adds genealogy and chronological reasoning concerning Khadijah’s grandson through her daughter Hind from an earlier marriage.

items.english_text:
7794—Muhammad ibn Sayfi [(2)]

Ibn Umayya ibn Abid ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn Makhzum.

Ibn al-Qaddah said: “He had Companionship.” Ibn Shahin mentioned him on the authority of [(3)] Abu Dawud. Abu Umar said: “He did not see the Prophet,” [(4)] and his status as a Companion is open to question. He was Khadijah bint Khuwaylid's grandson through her daughter. His mother was Hind bint Atiq ibn Amir ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn Makhzum, whose mother was Khadijah.

Abid is spelled with ba and an undotted dal.

I say: Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar mentioned something that strengthens Ibn al-Qaddah's position. When he mentioned Muhammad's father, he said: “He had [a son named] Rifa'a, after whom he took his kunya, and Sayfi ibn Umayya was killed on the day of Badr.” End quote.

A man whose father was killed at Badr—which occurred in the second year after the Emigration—would have lived for eight years or more during the Prophetic period. He would not have been named Muhammad unless his father and mother had embraced Islam. Perhaps, then, he was born after his father was killed, and his mother embraced Islam and named him Muhammad—or one of his relatives did so, if his mother died before he was named.

_________
[(2)] Usd al-Ghaba, entry 4742; al-Isti'ab, entry 2360; al-Thiqat, 3/365; al-Tarikh al-Kabir, 1/14; al-Kashif, 3/54; Talqih Fuhum Ahl al-Athar, 371; al-Jarh wa-l-Ta'dil, 7/287; al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, 2476; Tajrid Asma' al-Sahaba, 2/59; Baqi ibn Makhlad, 340.
[(3)] Manuscript A reads: “from Ibn Abi Dawud.”
[(4)] Manuscript A reads: “He has no narration.”

items.english_text:
8344—Mutahhar, a son of:

Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him), the master of humankind.

Ibn Zafar al-Hamawi mentioned him in his book al-Bishr bi-Khayr al-Bashar when enumerating the Prophet's children by Khadijah. He said: “Some people call him al-Tahir, but this is an error, for al-Tahir was the son of Abu Hala, and he too was Khadijah's son.” He did not mention his authority for this claim. But what would prevent Khadijah from naming one of her children by the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) after a son she had by another man? This occurs frequently among the Arabs. Others had preceded him in making that claim.

decisions.issue: Referent of وسبقه إلى ذلك غيره
decisions.resolution: Rendered it as others having preceded Ibn Zafar in making the claim.
decisions.basis: The sentence refers back to the disputed identification or naming assertion; no textual damage prevents this contextual rendering.

source.rationale: Records conflicting child lists and claims about identity, twin births, and the otherwise separately listed al-Mutayyab.

items.english_text:
In Ibn al-Barqi's History: “Khadijah bore the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) al-Qasim, Abd Allah, al-Tayyib, al-Tahir, and al-Mutahhar. It is said that al-Tayyib is identical with al-Tahir, namely Abd Allah. It is also said that al-Tayyib and al-Mutayyab were born from one pregnancy, and that al-Tahir and al-Mutahhar were born from one pregnancy.” A further notice of al-Tahir has already appeared above.

8345—Al-Mutayyab, son of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him):

He was mentioned in the preceding entry.

names.english: Abd Allah, son of the Prophet

decisions.issue: Meaning of ولدا في بطن
decisions.resolution: Rendered literally as “were born from one pregnancy.”
decisions.basis: This preserves the report's claim of a shared pregnancy without adding the explicit word “twins.”

decisions.resolution: Rendered as “A further notice of al-Tahir has already appeared above.”
decisions.basis: The phrase points to an earlier, additional treatment of al-Tahir rather than introducing a new factual claim.

source.rationale: Entry 9028 is not selected and adds substantive genealogical, transmission, and death information about Khadijah’s grandson.

items.english_text:
9028—Hind ibn Hind

Ibn [(1)] Abi Hala, the son of the subject of the preceding entry. According to Qatada and those who followed him, there would thus be three successive generations bearing the name Hind.

Ibn Manda mentioned him and cited, by way of Hassan ibn Abd Allah al-Wasiti, from al-Sari ibn Yahya, from Malik ibn Dinar: “Hind, son of Khadijah, the wife of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), related to me, saying: The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) passed by al-Hakam, the father of Marwan. Al-Hakam began making mocking gestures at the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and pointing with his finger, until the Prophet turned toward him and said: ‘O God, cause him to tremble’—meaning a bodily tremor. He immediately began trembling where he stood.”

Ibn Abi Hatim al-Razi likewise transmitted it by this route, as did Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Ziyadat al-Zuhd. Malik ibn Dinar did not meet Hind ibn Abi Hala; he met only his son. It is therefore as though he attributed the son to his grandfather.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from his father that Hind ibn Hind's narration from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) is mursal. Abu Umar followed the wording's apparent sense and assigned this hadith to Hind ibn Abi Hala.

Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar and al-Dulabi transmitted, by way of Muhammad ibn al-Hajjaj, from a man of the Banu Tamim, who said: “I saw Hind ibn Hind ibn Abi Hala wearing a green outfit. He died during the plague, and because the people were occupied with their own dead, four men carried him out. A woman cried: ‘Alas for Hind ibn Hind! Alas for the son of the Messenger of God's stepson!’ The people then crowded around his funeral procession and left their own dead.”

names.arabic: هند بن هند بن أبي هالة
names.english: Hind ibn Hind ibn Abi Hala

decisions.issue: Meaning of ثلاثة في نسق
decisions.resolution: Corrected the wording to “three successive generations bearing the name Hind.”
decisions.basis: The Arabic counts three persons named Hind in genealogical succession; it does not say that the full patronymic “Hind ibn Abi Hind” recurs three times.

decisions.issue: Association of Ziyadat al-Zuhd
decisions.resolution: Rephrased the sentence so that the work title modifies Abd Allah ibn Ahmad alone.
decisions.basis: In the Arabic, “in Ziyadat al-Zuhd” is specifically attached to Abd Allah ibn Ahmad, while Ibn Abi Hatim is a separate transmitter.
